title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.1
summary: Specifies version 1.1 of the Transport Layer Security protocol, which lets client and server applications communicate in ways designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering, and message forgery. It obsoleted RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0). It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 5246.

eli5.summary: A sealed-envelope system for the internet: only the person you write to can read the message, and nobody can change it. This is an old version, 1.1.

questions: what is an explicit iv in tls
subtitle: TLS 1.1 patched CBC weaknesses in TLS 1.0 and kept the same handshake and record design.

tldr.problem: Two applications talking over the Internet need privacy and data integrity, and TLS 1.0 had weaknesses in how it used CBC encryption.
tldr.mechanism: TLS 1.1 keeps the two-layer design, a Record Protocol for protecting data and a Handshake Protocol for agreeing on keys, and swaps the implicit CBC initialization vector for an explicit one and changes padding error handling.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4346 is Historic. It obsoleted RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and was itself obsoleted by RFC 5246.

today: RFC 4346 is Historic. It was obsoleted by RFC 5246, and it obsoleted RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0). It was also updated by RFC 4366, RFC 4680, RFC 4681, RFC 5746, RFC 6176, RFC 7465, RFC 7507, RFC 7919 and RFC 10015.

sections.title: What TLS 1.1 Provides
sections.content:
The primary goal of the TLS protocol is to provide privacy and data integrity between two communicating applications. It has two layers. At the bottom, on top of some reliable transport such as TCP, is the TLS Record Protocol. It keeps the connection private with symmetric encryption, using keys generated uniquely for each connection, and keeps it reliable with a keyed message authentication code (MAC).

Above it sits the TLS Handshake Protocol. It lets the client and server authenticate each other with public-key cryptography, negotiate a shared secret that eavesdroppers cannot obtain, and do so in a way where tampering with the negotiation is detected. TLS is application protocol independent: higher-level protocols layer on top of it, but the RFC leaves it to their designers to decide how to start a handshake and how to interpret certificates.

The goals, in order of priority, are cryptographic security, interoperability, extensibility and relative efficiency. TLS 1.1, TLS 1.0 and SSL 3.0 do not interoperate, although each has a mechanism for backing down to prior versions.
sections.eli5: TLS puts your message in a locked box that only the receiver can open, and adds a seal that breaks if anyone tampers with it.

sections.title: What Changed From TLS 1.0
sections.content:
The RFC describes TLS 1.1 as a revision of TLS 1.0 with small security improvements, clarifications and editorial improvements. The major changes are:

  • The implicit initialization vector (IV) is replaced with an explicit IV, to protect against CBC attacks.
  • Padding errors are reported with the bad_record_mac alert rather than decryption_failed, also to protect against CBC attacks.
  • IANA registries are defined for protocol parameters.
  • Premature closes no longer make a session non-resumable.
  • Informational notes were added about new attacks on TLS.
sections.eli5: The old lock had a pattern an attacker could guess, so the new lock starts every message with a fresh random twist.

sections.title: The Record Protocol
sections.content:
The Record Protocol takes messages to send, fragments them into blocks, optionally compresses them, applies a MAC, encrypts, and transmits the result. Received data is decrypted, verified, decompressed and reassembled. A record carries a type, a version, a length and the fragment. Records hold at most 2^14 bytes of plaintext, and TLS 1.1 uses version { 3, 2 }, which is historical because it descends from SSL 3.0.

Four record types are defined: change_cipher_spec (20), alert (21), handshake (22) and application_data (23). Each connection has current and pending read and write states, and the change cipher spec message makes the pending state current. Sequence numbers are 64-bit, start at zero and are included in the MAC, so missing, extra or repeated records can be detected.

For CBC block ciphers, each record starts with an explicit IV. Padding may be up to 255 bytes and every padding byte holds the padding length. Receivers must check the padding and SHOULD use the bad_record_mac alert for padding errors. Implementations must also make record processing time essentially the same whether or not the padding is correct, to resist a timing attack.
sections.eli5: Your message is cut into pieces, each piece gets a tamper seal and goes into a locked envelope, and the envelopes are numbered so a missing one is noticed.

sections.title: The Handshake
sections.content:
When a client and server first communicate, they agree on a protocol version and cryptographic algorithms, optionally authenticate each other, and use public-key techniques to produce shared secrets. The client sends a ClientHello and the server must answer with a ServerHello. These establish the protocol version, session ID, cipher suite and compression method, and exchange two random values.

The server then sends its certificate if it is to be authenticated, and may send a server key exchange and a certificate request. After ServerHelloDone the client sends its own certificate if asked, then the ClientKeyExchange and, if it has a signing certificate, a CertificateVerify. Both sides send a ChangeCipherSpec followed by a Finished message under the new keys. Application data MUST NOT be sent before the first handshake completes.

A client can resume an earlier session by sending its session ID. If the server agrees, both sides send change cipher spec and Finished messages straight away and skip the rest. The RFC also warns that a man-in-the-middle can try to push peers down to the weakest method they support, so higher layers must know their own security requirements.
sections.eli5: The two computers first say hello and agree on which secret code to use. Then they prove who they are, make up a shared secret, and each says Ready, now we are talking in code.

sections.title: Alerts and Closing
sections.content:
Alert messages carry a level, warning (1) or fatal (2), and a description. A fatal alert ends the connection immediately, and the session identifier must be invalidated so that the failed session is never resumed. Defined descriptions include close_notify, unexpected_message, bad_record_mac, handshake_failure, bad_certificate, certificate_expired, unknown_ca, protocol_version and no_renegotiation.

To avoid a truncation attack, each party must send a close_notify before closing the write side of the connection, and the other party must answer with its own and close. As of TLS 1.1, failing to close properly no longer prevents resuming the session.
sections.eli5: If something goes wrong, a computer shouts the problem and hangs up. A polite goodbye lets the other side know the talk really ended and was not cut off by someone else.

sections.title: Keys, the PRF and Cipher Suites
sections.content:
TLS expands secrets with a pseudorandom function (PRF) built from HMAC with both MD5 and SHA-1. The secret is split into two halves, P_MD5 runs on one and P_SHA-1 on the other, and the outputs are combined with exclusive-or. This is meant to stay secure if either hash remains secure.

The master secret is always exactly 48 bytes and is computed as PRF(pre_master_secret, "master secret", ClientHello.random + ServerHello.random). With RSA, the client generates a 48-byte pre_master_secret, encrypts it under the server's public key and sends it. With Diffie-Hellman, the negotiated value is used as the pre_master_secret. The record layer's MAC secrets and write keys are then derived from the master secret by the PRF with the label key expansion.

Unless an application profile says otherwise, a compliant application MUST implement the cipher suite TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA. The security considerations section only points to appendices D, E and F, which cover implementation notes, backward compatibility with SSL and a security analysis.
sections.eli5: Both sides mix their secret with two random numbers they swapped earlier, and out come the same set of keys on each side, like two people following the same recipe.
